passage:
Tenzin silenced his phone again. Reminders for the card due date, the bike EMI and a buy-now-pay-later plan for a jacket kept arriving, and he had told no one. That night he wrote every amount on paper. The total made his stomach drop, but seeing it made it manageable. He put the card with the highest interest first, then told his older sister. She only said, "Thank you for telling me. Let us build a plan."

He had taken part of the loan to meet family expectations for a cousin's wedding. When his mother, Jaya, asked for more, he sat with her. "I want to help, but I can give this much until December. I do not want you thinking I have more than I do." Jaya was quiet, then nodded.

Temptation kept coming. A phone offer flashed, "Pay later, ten easy parts." He asked himself if it was a need, then left it in the basket for a week. By Saturday he had forgotten it.

And Kashish, who had borrowed a good sum from him in March, kept dodging his calls. Tenzin felt used. He wrote once: "I need this back by the month end. Can we set two payments?" Kashish sent half. Tenzin decided he would lend only what he could afford to lose.

qa.q: Whom did Tenzin tell first about his debts?
qa.a: He told his older sister.

qa.q: How did Tenzin's approach to his hidden debt differ from how he handled Jaya's request and Kashish's dodging?
qa.a: With the debt he wrote every amount down, put the high-interest card first and told his sister. With Jaya he talked openly about a limit. With Kashish he asked once, clearly, with a plan, and decided to lend only what he could afford to lose.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling about his debts before he told anyone?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and alone with a heavy secret, and his stomach dropped when he saw the total.

qa.q: How did Tenzin handle the pay-later offer for the phone?
qa.a: He asked himself if it was a need and left it in the basket for a week, by which time he had forgotten it.

grounding: Debt shows up as a hidden burden, a loan taken partly for family expectations, tempting easy credit, and a friend who dodges repayment.

passage:
At Sunday lunch, Neelam's aunt Gargi banged her spoon. "You students are brainwashed!" Neelam's ears went hot and she wanted to snap back. She said, "I would rather not argue while we are both heated, Aunty. Can we talk after lunch?" and asked about the pickles instead. The rest of lunch survived.

Her fear was real, though. She believed the other side's win could wreck the library programmes and environmental rules she valued. That week she read three sources from different sides, noticed one channel that seemed to want her scared, and signed up to volunteer at the local library drive.

At a debate society meeting, Neelam admired a leader from her own party, and her chest swelled when the leader spoke. Then a classmate pointed out a flaw in one policy. She felt defensive, but she said, "That is a fair point. I will look at the numbers."

Jaya, from the rival club, sat opposite. Instead of scoring points, Neelam asked, "How did you come to that view?" Jaya described growing up beside a town where jobs disappeared. They both realised they wanted people to have steady work and clean air, and disagreed about how. They left with a plan to write a short list of shared goals.

qa.q: What did Neelam ask about at lunch instead of arguing?
qa.a: She asked about the pickles.

qa.q: How did Aunt Gargi share her view compared with how Jaya shared hers?
qa.a: Gargi banged her spoon and said students are brainwashed, while Jaya, when Neelam asked, described growing up beside a town where jobs disappeared and left with a plan to list shared goals.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when her aunt shouted that students are brainwashed?
qa.a: She felt insulted and angry, and wanted to snap back.

qa.q: How did Neelam act on her fear of the other side winning?
qa.a: She read three sources from different sides, noticed a channel that seemed to want her scared, and volunteered at the local library drive.

grounding: Political talk brings a shouting relative, fear of the other side winning, admiration for a leader tempered by a fair criticism, and curiosity that finds shared values.

passage:
On Monday Sonali opened the class group chat and saw a meme with her face pasted onto a cartoon pig. Her cheeks burned. More laughing faces kept arriving. She took a screenshot, blocked the sender and told her mother that night.

Then an account with no name began sending nasty messages. Sonali caught herself staring at ten possible classmates, testing each guess. Zubin said, "Do not do that. Let us report it." They saved the messages and reported the account to the platform and to the school counsellor next morning. The counsellor promised to speak to the class teacher the same day.

Sonali's first impulse was to post a nastier meme in return. She typed half of it, then deleted it. Revenge would only feed the fire, she thought, and the screenshots were better.

By Wednesday her stomach cramped whenever she saw the school gate. She told her mother, "I don't want to go." Her mother sat beside her, did not argue, and phoned the school office. The next day the counsellor met Sonali with the head. Tanvir sat with her at lunch. "This is not your fault." By Friday the account was closed.

qa.q: What was Sonali's face pasted onto in the meme?
qa.a: It was pasted onto a cartoon pig.

qa.q: How did Sonali's first impulse after the meme differ from what she actually did about the anonymous account and her dread of school?
qa.a: She wanted to post a nastier meme, but she deleted it, saved screenshots, reported the account with Zubin, and told her mother and the counsellor about her dread.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling when her stomach cramped at the sight of the school gate?
qa.a: She felt dread and fear about going to school because of what was online.

qa.q: What did Zubin suggest when Sonali stared at possible classmates?
qa.a: Zubin suggested reporting the account instead of guessing who it was.

grounding: One teenager is mocked with memes and messages from an anonymous account, feels angry and afraid, and turns to evidence, reporting and trusted adults.

passage:
Kunal forwarded a message to his housing-society group: "Tanker supply stops tomorrow, store water now!" It was false, and by evening neighbours were queuing at shops and Mrs Rao was in tears. Kunal deleted the message, posted a correction in the same group, and apologised to Mrs Rao by name. Afterwards he made a rule: check two sources before forwarding.

His friend Chaitanya went the other way. After being lied to several times, Chaitanya said, "All news is fake." Kunal shook his head. "If you trust nothing, anyone can tell you anything. Keep a few sources that correct their errors." Chaitanya grumbled but bookmarked two.

Zainab noticed her feed made her angry every night. Her mood was sour, and her opinions felt narrower. She unfollowed a dozen accounts, set a no-phone hour before bed, and read one long article every Sunday. "Outrage is what they reward," she told Kunal.

During the election campaign a clip went round showing a candidate seeming to mock farmers. Zainab watched the full speech and saw the clip had been edited. "Who benefits from us being furious?" she asked.

qa.q: What did the false message say?
qa.a: It said, "Tanker supply stops tomorrow, store water now!"

qa.q: How did Chaitanya's distrust differ from Kunal's new rule and Zainab's habits?
qa.a: Chaitanya decided all news is fake, which leaves anyone free to fool him. Kunal checks two sources before forwarding. Zainab curates her feed, watches the full speech, and asks who benefits.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when neighbours queued at the shops and Mrs Rao was in tears?
qa.a: He felt guilty and ashamed of the panic his forward had caused.

qa.q: What did Kunal do to repair the harm of his false forward?
qa.a: He deleted the message, posted a correction in the same group and apologised to Mrs Rao by name.

grounding: A false forward causes panic, a friend swings to distrusting all news, another notices her feed hooks her with outrage, and an edited campaign clip shows how emotion is steered.

passage:
After Papa moved into a flat across town, Ira found herself crying at odd moments: over toast at breakfast, during maths, once at the school gate. She missed the noisy Sunday dinners. She kept her routines, drew a picture of the four of them, and told her teacher about it.

For weeks she planned ways to fix things: a card for both parents, a cake for their anniversary, a scheme for one long holiday together. Nothing changed, and her mother, Shalini, said gently, "We love you both, and we cannot be together again. It is not your job to fix it." Ira threw the card on the floor and slammed her bedroom door. "You ruined everything!" she shouted at Mum, then at Papa on the phone. Afterwards she ran around the yard until her legs ached and wrote in her diary, "I am sad and angry."

Shalini's new friend Binita brought mangoes and asked if Ira wanted to help peel them. Ira said, "No," and turned away. She was afraid Binita would take Papa's place. Shalini said, "Okay, you do not have to." Binita nodded. "I am here whenever." Over the months Ira said hello politely and kept her Saturdays with Papa. One day she passed Binita the peeler without a word, and both left it at that.

qa.q: What did Binita bring?
qa.a: Binita brought mangoes.

qa.q: How did Ira's plans to fix things differ from where they led, and how did her feeling toward Binita change?
qa.a: Her plans, a card, a cake and a holiday scheme, did not change anything, and hearing it was not her job to fix it left her sad and angry, so she slammed her door, ran around the yard and wrote in her diary. With Binita she began by saying no, stayed polite, and later passed the peeler without a word.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she slammed her bedroom door and shouted at her parents?
qa.a: She felt angry, with sadness underneath, because she believed they had ruined the home.

qa.q: How did Ira let out her anger in a way that hurt nobody?
qa.a: She ran around the yard until her legs ached and wrote in her diary that she was sad and angry.

grounding: After her parents separate, one child cries at odd moments, plans to bring them back together, slams doors in anger, and slowly warms to her mother's new friend.

passage:
Nirmala, twenty-four, tried every street snack in her new northern city and asked the cook how the spices were toasted. She adopted the local habit of arriving five minutes early to meetings, but kept her Sunday puja and her mother tongue on calls.

At work, a colleague mimicked her accent at lunch and others grinned. It stung. She told herself: their bias is not my defect. She said calmly, "I would prefer you not do that." The colleague shrugged, but later Nitin from finance sat with her. "That was not okay. I noted it for HR if you want to use it." She wrote down the date.

In the first months, evenings were long. She missed her mother's sambar, easy jokes and the noise. Feeling lonely was common early on, she told herself. She joined a running club, invited two colleagues to weekend brunch, called home every Sunday, and gave herself until spring.

Her mother, Sarita, lived alone. Nirmala felt guilty and torn. She set two calls a week, planned a visit in November, asked a neighbour to look in daily, and told her mother honestly what she could not do. "Love can travel," said Sarita.

qa.q: What did Nirmala join to meet people?
qa.a: She joined a running club.

qa.q: How did Nirmala's curiosity differ from the colleague's mimicry, and how did she handle loneliness and guilt?
qa.a: Her curiosity welcomed new food and customs, while the mimicry stung and she answered it calmly with Nitin's support. For loneliness she joined a club and gave herself until spring, and for guilt she set calls, planned a visit and arranged for a neighbour to look in.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling during the long evenings of her first months?
qa.a: She felt lonely, missing her mother's sambar, easy jokes and the noise of home.

qa.q: What could Nirmala do about guilt over her mother living alone?
qa.a: She could act on it, as she did, with regular calls, a planned visit and local support, and be honest about her limits.

grounding: A move to a new city brings curiosity about customs, a colleague's accent mockery, early loneliness, and guilt about a mother living far away.
